translations.text: The Life of Our Beloved Brother Apa Paul of Tamma, who went to his rest on the seventh day of the month of Paopi. May his blessing come upon us, and may we be saved in the peace of God. Amen. Listen, you who love to listen, to the voice [?] worthy [?], as he said to his disciples, “If you keep my commandments [?], you will remain in them [?].” [?] God sent Michael the archangel to me at noon on the sixteenth day of Epip. He said to me, “Greetings, my honored son.” I answered him, “Greetings, [?].” [?] is the man from Tamma, for you are the one who will take charge of his body when he lays his body down.
When he had said these things, he went to heaven in glory. I immediately got up and stopped under [?] [?].

[?] is equal. John said, “Let him be our father and our bishop in these matters.” Peter said, “My father Paul, get up and call upon God to send us bread from heaven so that we may eat together.” My father said, “Forgive me. Bless me. Get up, and let us pray to him, and he will listen to us.” They got up and stretched out their hands together. My father called upon God, saying, “My Lord Jesus Christ, you who blessed five loaves, so that five hundred people ate and were sustained by the five barley loaves and the two fish; you who listened to Elisha and satisfied a thousand people with ten barley loaves: listen to me today. You who listened to Daniel when he was in the lions’ den and sent Habakkuk to him with the meal in his hands: listen to me today and send me bread from heaven so that I may eat with my brothers and my fathers.” Immediately, a table appeared with a dish on it, and on the dish were three warm loaves. They were set down among us. My father said to them, “Get up, and let us eat the bread of heaven.”

He also took a little salt and put it on the table. We prayed together and ate the little bread with the Lord’s blessing. My father answered and said to the brothers, “I tell you, it has been fifty-four years from the day my head was shaved on the mountain by my beloved father, Apa Hyperichus, until now. One loaf of bread and one measure of water are allotted to me by God every forty days. I do not know where they come from. I eat some of them on the evening of my fortieth day, and I do not eat again until the completion of my next forty days, according to the Savior’s command, which he gave us in the holy Gospel. He himself neither ate nor drank for forty days and forty nights.” The brothers said to him, “You do well. An athlete does not receive a crown unless he competes well.” He raised his hands toward heaven and prayed with the brothers, saying, “Lord Jesus Christ, King of kings, hear us today and send us bread that is warm and fresh.” Immediately, behold, [?] came from heaven and settled in our midst, wrapped in linen cloths. Peter said to John, “Here are the bread and the cloths. We also need the preparations for the offering.” John answered and said to the brothers, “Pray for me so that I may do what he [?].” [?] John opened his mouth and said, “Our Lord Jesus Christ, send a table from heaven so that we may place your body and your blood on it.” Immediately, behold, a golden table came from heaven and settled in our midst. Paul also stood up and prayed in this way, saying, “My Lord Jesus Christ, you who called me to the lot of the holy apostles, although I was formerly a persecutor, persecuting his holy bride, the Church,

“Now then, Lord, hear me in the midst of my brothers and send me from heaven a cup full of wine from the true vine.” At that moment, behold, a cup full of wine from the true vine settled on the table. The elder Apa Isidore, the priest, also stood up. He raised both his hands toward heaven and prayed, saying, “Lord God Almighty, King of kings, I am not worthy to speak in the midst of my brothers and these chosen ones of yours whom you chose for yourself as apostles. But because of the joy you have given me, I have stood up and called upon you. Listen to me and send me incense from the incense of Paradise, so that we may offer it while we invoke your name over your holy body and blood.” Immediately, behold, a bowl full of incense settled in the midst of us, and we breathed in the incense. Apa Agathonicus, of the mountain of [?], also stood up. [?] He said, [?].
[?] crumbs that remained of [?] were being put into my father’s basket. I drank the water in the measure. We prayed and left that place. We went south through the whole mountain. [?]

[?] the brothers who were monks. We heard a voice saying, “[?] bless us, Apa Paul of Tamma and Ezekiel of the little cell. Come in, saints of the Lord. Welcome to us, Apa Paul of Tamma, whom the Lord raised up [?] you in this place today.” My father said, “Greetings to you, Apa Pamun, who wears the robe of many colors [?] colors, like Joseph, the righteous king.” He asked him again, “Who shaved your head?” He said, “It was my father, Apa Hellen. Remember me, my holy father.” [?] my father [?] “Where do you usually gather for worship on Saturday and Sunday?” Apa Pamun answered, “John the virgin is the one who usually gathers for worship on Saturday and Sunday. For on Saturday [?].

We found Apa Apollo sitting on a throne, teaching his children the commandments of life. When he saw my father, Apa Paul, he rose from his throne, embraced him, and kissed him. He said, “Welcome to us today, bridegroom of Christ, Apa Paul, whom the Lord has raised from the dead five times. He will raise you again, as he told you, and the seventh time he raises you will be on the day of the resurrection of all the saints.”

After Apa Apollo had said these things, he had all the people assembled and went to the church. We gathered for the holy offering. He left the brothers in the dining room, but took us to the service room and had food prepared for us to eat. My father, however, did not want to eat, because he had spent three days fasting in the wilderness. Our father Apa Apollo stood up and urged him, saying, “Listen to me, my father, and eat with me, so that a blessing may come upon my dwelling and my monastery today because of you. You know, my beloved father, that what enters a person’s mouth is not what defiles that person. So now, my father, listen to me and eat with me.” My father then agreed to eat with Apa Apollo. My brother and I also ate together, along with the other brothers who were with us, whose names were Apa Paese, Apa Nischroou, Apa Sures, and Apa Pitta. When we finished eating in the evening, our father Apa Apollo came among us and clapped his hands together, saying, “Let whoever has received wings fly away.” At that moment Apa Paese flew away and hurried to the mountain of Hache.

Apa Nischroou also flew away and went to the mountain north of Antinoë. Apa Pitta also flew away and went to the mountain of Asyut. At dawn, our father Apa Apollo accompanied us out toward the south, to the monastery. He greeted us and sent us away in peace. We walked south through the whole mountain region until we came to the mountain of Terotashans, south of Qus. Down below, we found gazelles grazing, with a monk among them. My father went forward, greeted him, and said to him, “What is your name?” He said, “My name is Aphou. Remember me, my father Apa Paul, so that the Lord may bring me to a good end.” My father said to him, “How many years have you been in this place?” He said, “Fifty-four years.” My father said to him again, “Who clothed you in the monastic habit?” He said, “Apa Anthony of Scetis.” My father said to him, “Then what do you live on as you travel with these gazelles?” He said, “My food and the food of these gazelles are the same: the plants of the field and these wild greens.” My father said to him, “Do you not get cold in winter or suffer from the heat in summer?” He said to him, “In winter I sleep among these gazelles, and they warm me with the breath from their mouths. In summer they gather together and stand over me, shading me so that the scorching heat does not trouble me.” My father said to him, “Truly, you deserve to be called Apa Aphou the Gazelle.”
At that moment a voice came to us, saying, “This is his name throughout all the generations of the earth.”
We were amazed at what had happened so quickly. We greeted him, left him, and walked south to the mountain of Pshchepohe. We found a dwelling to our west.
My father knocked on the stone three times, according to the rule of the monastic brothers.
Immediately we heard a faint voice saying, “Bless me, my holy fathers.”
Then he came out and opened the door for us. We bowed down before him and greeted him.
His body had become extremely thin from hunger and thirst. He took us into the dwelling. We prayed, sat down, and spoke about the mighty deeds of God.
My father said to him, “What is your name?”
He answered, saying, “My name is Phib, and I am from Perchous in the district of Touho.”
My father said to him, “How many years has it been since you came to this place?”
He said, “It has been eighteen years [?].”
My father said to him, “How long will you remain in this place?”
He said to him again, “This is my dwelling in life and in death.”
My father said to him, “What do you eat, or what do you drink, or who attends to your needs?”
The holy Apa Phib answered, “From the time of my childhood, when I left my home, until today,
wherever I live, each time I complete my forty-day fast, I find a loaf of bread and a jug of water set before me.
“And God is my witness that, since that time, only one loaf has been allotted to me each time.”
But when you came to me today with your disciple, look, God sent us food for the three of us.
Now get up, and let us taste a little bread, as God has commanded.”

We got up, stretched out our hands, and prayed. We stretched ourselves out and ate together from a single loaf. We also drank a little water. We left our father Apa Phoeb, and he sent us on our way in peace.
We traveled south through the whole mountain region until we came to Mount Meroit, and we found ourselves a place to live there.
I was sitting alone in the dwelling when a man came to the door and called to me.
I went outside to see what was happening.
He said to me, “Are you Ezekiel?”
I said to him, “Yes, I am.”
He said to me, “Let me inside the door of your dwelling so that I can tell you this matter.
I do not want to say it where the brothers might hear and become frightened.”
Because of his pleasant way of speaking, I took him inside.
He said to me, “My brother Ezekiel, do you know what has happened?”
I said, “No.”

He said to me, “Yesterday at the seventh hour, I was walking in the desert with some other men, looking for stones to make into lime [?]. We encountered robbers in the mountains, and they took our tools from us. We barely managed to escape from them alive.
When we escaped from their hands, we came upon a large man, tied up and lying in a valley.
We untied him.”

He said to us, “Leave me here. But when you go to the mountain, you will find the dwelling place. Call inside, ‘Ezekiel, your father says, “Come to me in the desert, for the robbers rose up and bound me, wanting to kill me, but God rescued my soul from their hands.”’”
We asked him, “What is your name?”
He said to us, “My name is Paul, and I am from Tamma in the district of Kois.”
When I, Ezekiel, heard these things, I was shaken because he had spoken my father’s name and the name of his village.
That man said to me again, “Get up and follow me, and I will take you to him, for I see that you are afraid.”
I walked with him throughout the desert. I spent the first day and the second day walking.
I said to him, “Have we not yet reached that place?”
He said, “No. We had reached the third [?] day of walking in the desert.”
I said to him again, “Have we still not reached him?”
He said, “Look, we have come close to him.”
While he was speaking with me, he changed and became a huge Ethiopian. His eyes were full of blood, his whole body was covered with hair, and he stank like billy goats.
He said to me, “Did you not recognize me, Ezekiel?”
I said to him, “No.” He said to me, “I was the one making the spring run dry at that time. Your father struck me until I filled it again as it had been before.
I suffered when I rose against you and your father, but you did not become wise.”
I said to him, “So you are the devil! May the Lord rebuke you for all the evil things you have done to Christ’s servants.”
He lunged after me like a wild lion, wanting to kill me.
But I cried out, “My father, help me!”
Immediately my father heard my voice as though he were close to me. He got up at once and came to me through God’s help.

When my father approached him, the devil immediately changed and took the appearance of a monk, wearing a skin and small palm-leaf garments. He bowed to my father and fell at his feet according to the custom of the monastic brothers.
Immediately my father struck him around the side of his monastic robe, [?], because he recognized that he was the devil.
He seized him, bound him hand and foot, and rolled him down into a ditch. We left him and went away.
I said to my father, “What is this thing you have done to this shameless creature?”
My father said to me, “God has handed him over to me so that I may punish him as I wish, because he dared to tempt us.”
After my father said these things, we got up and returned to our dwelling, giving glory to God.

My father spent forty days and forty nights without eating or drinking, sitting on a brick inside the dwelling and staring at a window through an opening. He did not close his eyes during these forty days, until they burst and fell out onto the ground.

The holy archangel—that is, Michael the archangel—came from heaven at daybreak on Sunday, at the completion of the forty days. He marked him with the seal and relieved him of all his sufferings, and his eyes were restored to their proper condition. Michael the archangel went up to heaven in glory.
We gathered with the brothers who were with us in that place and ate with them on Sunday. Then we left them in peace.
We went south to the rock of Asyut and obtained a small dwelling for ourselves there.
My father practiced great acts of ascetic discipline.
One day a great saint of God came to us. His name was Apa Bishoy of Jeremiah, and he lived in the mountain of Qaw, east of the river.
We greeted one another, prayed, and sat down. We spoke about the mighty deeds of Christ and the ways of life of the saints.
When they had finished arguing with one another, we got up and walked in the mountain. We found a rock full of bones. They were all idol worshipers.
When the saints reached them, they stood and prayed over them. They all rose alive, numbering six hundred men and fifty-four women.
The saints said to them, “What is your occupation?”
One of them answered, saying, “Listen to me, holy ones, and I will tell you about our wickedness and our lawlessness.
For we are a single nation, worshiping a wild animal called the wolf. We care for it at all times, offering it little children three years old as sacrifices.
It encouraged us, saying, ‘Do things like this for me,’ and other deeds worse than these, which we do not wish to speak of.
Now, therefore, my holy fathers, let your mercy reach us and baptize us as Christians, for the distress upon us is great.”
Christ’s bridegroom, Apa Bishoy of Jeremiah, answered, “Get up, and let us pray to God so that he may give us assurance concerning this matter.”
My father said, “Let us pray.”

They got up and called upon God together, saying, “Merciful and compassionate God, who sent his only Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, who died for his creation and freed the world through the blessing of holy baptism: have compassion on these servants of yours who stand here today, looking expectantly for your mercy and compassion, so that they may receive forgiveness [?].
